1:
Who Sargon was splits the older readers from the two who had the excavations. Adam Clarke thinks Sennacherib is meant, possibly under one of the seven names an early father says he bore, and notes two further names given him in the Apocrypha. John Calvin argues the same from the general named here being one of Sennacherib's captains, which constrains us to acknowledge that this king had two names; John Wesley equates them; Matthew Henry leaves it open between Sennacherib and his predecessor. Charles Ellicott answers from the monuments: before their discovery the name appeared nowhere but here and his very existence had been questioned, whereas he now stands out as one of the greatest Assyrian monarchs, who succeeded the conqueror of Samaria first as co-regent and then in his own name until Sennacherib followed. Keil and Delitzsch press it further: Sargon and not his predecessor took Samaria after a three years' siege and boasted of carrying away the house of Omri, the predecessor died before the city while Sargon seized the throne after a contest with the lawful heirs, and he was therefore a usurper, so the old identification can no longer stand.

The general's name is treated the same way. Ellicott makes it not a name but the official title of the commander-in-chief, next in authority to the king, who may or may not be the officer of that rank sent later to Jerusalem, and dates the campaign from the annals, where an Ashdod king refused tribute and was deposed for his brother. John Gill takes it for a personal name, gives the Greek and Arabic forms, and makes its bearer one of Sennacherib's generals.

Henry dates the prophecy by the siege itself, an event so remarkable that those living then could fix the year by it, and notes that the prophet had already been a sign in the sackcloth he had long worn, which some take him to have put on when the ten tribes were carried away and others to have been his ordinary dress. Adam Clarke adds that the town was strong, holding out twenty-nine years against an Egyptian king long afterwards.

How long the prophet went stripped is the chapter's real dispute. Clarke thinks it improbable that he walked uncovered three years, and argues that three whole years of it could give no premonition of the time, whereas three days would, a day standing for a year by the prophetic rule; he suggests either that the words for three days dropped out of the text after barefoot, or that a Greek translator read years for days. Ellicott takes the opposite view, that month by month for three whole years the prophet was seen in the streets as one already a prisoner of war, and that there are no adequate grounds for limiting the action to a day or three days.

On what nakedness meant they agree. Ellicott identifies the sackcloth as the rough garment the prophets habitually wore and confines the nakedness to laying that robe aside and appearing in the short tunic, listing the horns, the yokes and the binding girdle as like instances of prophesying in act. Wesley says the same, without the upper garment as slaves and prisoners went, and barefoot as mourners and captives did. Calvin draws a rule from it: had the prophet done this of his own accord he would have been justly ridiculed, but done at God's command it can only excite awe; and since God never acts without explaining his reason, the prophet states the design as well as walking. False prophets imitate this, putting on varied and imposing shapes to dazzle the eyes of the multitude and gain credit for themselves, but their symbols are worthless because God is not their author, which he makes the rule for meeting those who offer empty ceremonies in place of true sacraments.
3:
Why three years is answered by three of them. John Wesley says the term was not served constantly but only when the prophet went abroad among the people for whom the sign was appointed. Charles Ellicott holds that the sign was made in act and in silence, its meaning left unfolded until the years ran out, and notes that Egypt and Ethiopia stand connected here as in the two preceding chapters, both being under a king of Ethiopian stock. John Calvin gives the reason for the length: it was the truce granted those nations for repentance, and a trial of the obedience of God's own people, that they might relinquish unlawful aid at once and know that a security which looked so attractive was not far from ruin. The spectacle also exposed the rebellion of the wicked, who displayed their impiety openly in despising the prophet's nakedness, while the godly looked past it to the mark the Lord had set upon it. John Gill notes only that the explanation of the sign now follows.

The captivity is given historically by one and morally by the rest. Ellicott observes that the prediction was fulfilled under neither Sargon nor Sennacherib but under a later king who subdued the whole of Egypt and set satraps over its provinces, and that the prophet paints in vivid colours the brutality with which prisoners were treated on the march. Wesley notes that the garments were cut off by the middle, Calvin that the words for captivity are collective and no distinction of age is made. Gill has those who trusted these nations afraid their turn is next and ashamed of having trusted at all.

Keil and Delitzsch put the question the passage turns on: if Egypt and Ethiopia are so shamefully humbled, what impression will it make on those who leaned upon a power supposed unapproachable and invincible? They render the cry as a discovery of having been deceived by the one nation looked to and the other gloried in, ending with the despairing how shall we ourselves escape. Ellicott adds two confirmations from outside: the Assyrian officer's scornful phrase about a bruised reed seems to imply Assyria had ceased to fear Egyptian power, and a later prophet speaks of Thebes as already conquered and its people carried away.

Calvin states for whose benefit the oracle about foreigners was given: that the Jews might learn in their afflictions to hope in God, and not have recourse to the foreign aid the Lord had forbidden. Wesley agrees that although the words are general the Israelites are principally intended, and closes with the confession the verse puts in their mouth, that so vain is a hope placed on a people unable to deliver themselves.

As for the isle that speaks at the close, Gill follows the rabbis in taking it for the land of Israel, which bordered the sea and was in any case cut off from other countries, and reports the opinion that Jerusalem is meant and that the word means simply a region, watered or not. Ellicott renders it coast-land and refers it to the whole seaboard, Philistia foremost in the revolt with Phoenicia and perhaps Cyprus, who would learn too late that they could not resist Assyria even with Egyptian help. Calvin extends the name to the whole of Judea and not Jerusalem only, doubting the usual reason that its shores are washed by the Mediterranean; he remarks that in Hebrew to look often means to hope, since we turn our eyes to whatever quarter we expect help from, censures the wandering levity of a people who should have looked to God alone, and turns the warning on his readers, that if we are invited by God and refuse the sure refuge he offers, letting ourselves be captivated by the delusions of Satan, we shall deservedly lie down naked and destitute with shame.
